Item-restscore association

Source: R/item_restscore.R
RMitemrestscore.Rd

Computes, for each item, the observed and model-expected association between the item and the rest score (the total score on the other items), measured by Goodman-Kruskal's gamma with iarm::item_restscore(). Reports their signed difference, the item's location relative to the mean person location, and a misfit flag. With the result of RMitemRestscoreCutoff(), items are flagged on a bootstrap p-value corrected across items, which is recommended over the default asymptotic test (see Details).

Usage

RMitemRestscore(
  data,
  cutoff = NULL,
  p_value = NULL,
  correction = c("fwer", "fdr_bh", "fdr_by", "none"),
  alpha = 0.05,
  output = "kable",
  sort,
  p_adj = "BH"
)

Arguments

data

A data.frame or matrix of item responses, items scored from 0. Missing values (NA) are allowed, but the statistic uses complete cases only, so at least one is needed.

cutoff

Optional. Default NULL, which tests each item with the asymptotic normal test of iarm::item_restscore(), adjusted by p_adj. Either of:

  • The full result of RMitemRestscoreCutoff(). This enables the bootstrap p-values (see p_value) and adds the columns Diff_low and Diff_high, the interval of the simulated differences.

  • Its $item_cutoffs data.frame alone (columns Item, diff_low, diff_high). Items are then flagged against the interval.

With a cutoff, the asymptotic p_adjusted column is dropped and p_adj is ignored.

p_value

Logical or NULL. Whether to flag on bootstrap p-values from the simulated values in cutoff. NULL (default) uses them whenever cutoff is the full RMitemRestscoreCutoff() result. TRUE without it is an error. With FALSE and a cutoff, items are flagged against the interval, and a one-time message gives the family-wise error rate that implies.

correction

Character. Correction of the bootstrap p-values across items: "fwer" (default, Westfall-Young step-down, controls the family-wise error rate), "fdr_bh" or "fdr_by" (Benjamini-Hochberg or Benjamini-Yekutieli, control the false discovery rate), or "none".

alpha

Numeric in (0, 1). An item is flagged when its corrected p-value is below alpha: the bootstrap p-value with a cutoff, the asymptotic one without. Default 0.05.

output

Character. "kable" (default) for a knitr::kable() table, or "dataframe".

sort

Optional. sort = "diff" sorts the rows by the absolute Difference, largest first, so that over- and underfitting items both come first. Other values leave the order unchanged.

p_adj

Character. Adjustment of the asymptotic p-values across items, passed to iarm::item_restscore(). Default "BH" (Benjamini-Hochberg). "none" gives unadjusted p-values, and any method of stats::p.adjust() can be used. Only used when cutoff = NULL.

Value

  • output = "kable": a knitr_kable table with the item name, the observed and expected gamma, their difference, the adjusted p-value, the Flagged label and the relative item location.

  • output = "dataframe": a data.frame with the columns Item, Observed, Expected, Difference, p_adjusted, Flagged and Relative_location. Flagged is "overfit" (observed above expected, adjusted p < alpha), "underfit" (below, adjusted p < alpha) or "".

With a cutoff, p_adjusted is replaced by Diff_low and Diff_high, followed by p_restscore (uncorrected equal-tailed bootstrap p) and padj_restscore (corrected p) when bootstrap p-values are used. Flagged then marks padj_restscore < alpha, or values outside the interval with p_value = FALSE.

Difference is observed minus expected gamma. Positive values mean the item is more strongly associated with the rest score than the model predicts (overfit, often from local dependence). Negative values mean a weaker association (underfit, often from multidimensionality or noise).

Details

Statistic. The item-restscore gamma (Kreiner, 2011) measures the association between the responses to one item and the rest score. Under the Rasch model the observed and expected gamma agree, apart from sampling error. The statistic is conditional on the total score.

Data and model. The item parameters are estimated by conditional maximum likelihood with psychotools::pcmodel() (a dichotomous item is a 2-category partial credit model). The statistic uses complete cases, and every response category must be used in them, or the function stops and names the item. The relative item location is the mean of the item's CML thresholds minus the mean WLE person location, a description of targeting. The iarm package must be installed (it is in Suggests).

The asymptotic p-value is miscalibrated. Without a cutoff, each item is tested with (observed - expected) / SE against the standard normal, where the SE is that of the observed gamma alone. The expected gamma is estimated from the same data and correlates with the observed one, so the SE is too large for the difference. The difference is also biased upwards in small samples. When the Rasch model holds, the test therefore flags too many items as overfit in small samples and too few as underfit at every sample size, and the adjustment in p_adj corrects neither. In simulation, 20 dichotomous items at n = 150 gave at least one BH-flagged item in 13% of datasets (30% when 1.5 logits off target), almost all of them overfit, while 9 polytomous items at n = 1000 gave about 1%. Pass the result of RMitemRestscoreCutoff() as cutoff for p-values from a parametric bootstrap instead. The simulation study is reported at https://pgmj.github.io/rasch_book/chapters/restscore-asymptotic-null.html.

Bootstrap p-values. Each item's observed Difference is compared with its simulated values from cutoff$results, studentised by the mean and SD of the observed and simulated values together. Subtracting that mean removes the small-sample bias of the difference, and dividing by that SD accounts for the correlation between the observed and expected gamma.

The test is equal-tailed: overfit and underfit each get alpha / 2. Gamma is bounded at 1, so the simulated Difference is skewed to the left, and a two-sided test on |t| would reject more often in the long (underfit) tail. The uncorrected p is twice the smaller of the one-sided Monte Carlo p-values, (1 + #{t* >= t}) / (B + 1) and (1 + #{t* <= t}) / (B + 1) for B simulated datasets, so it cannot be smaller than 2 / (B + 1). With correction = "fwer", the Westfall-Young step-down on the studentised maximum (Ferreira, 2024) is run once in each direction, and padj_restscore is twice the smaller of the two corrected p-values. "fdr_bh" and "fdr_by" adjust the equal-tailed uncorrected p-values.

In simulation with the Rasch model true, over four conditions (20 dichotomous or 9 polytomous items, n = 150 to 1000, on or off target), correction = "fwer" flagged at least one item in 5.0% of datasets, 2.4% underfit and 2.75% overfit. A test on |t| also held 5.0%, but split it 3.7% and 1.6%. The equal-tailed test also gave fewer false underfit flags when other items overfit (4.7% against 6.2% with two overfitting items), at a cost of 2 to 3 percentage points of power to detect underfitting items. Before easyRasch2 1.4.0.9004 the test was on |t|.

Reproducibility. The bootstrap p-values depend on the simulations, so two analyses of the same data with different seeds can disagree about items near the decision boundary. In simulation, in conditions chosen to include such items, two seeds disagreed about the flag of at least one item in about 10% of analyses at 400 iterations and 6% at 1000 with correction = "fwer", and in 13% and 11% with "fdr_bh". Set seed in RMitemRestscoreCutoff() for a reproducible analysis, and use 1000 or more iterations for a final one.

The direction in Flagged follows the studentised value, not the sign of Difference. At small sample sizes the simulated Difference has a slightly positive mean, so an item can, rarely, be flagged "underfit" while its Difference is just above zero.

Multiple comparisons

The uncorrected p-value controls the error rate of a single comparison. For one item (or item pair) chosen in advance it is the relevant value. Flagging whichever of k comparisons fall below alpha tests k hypotheses at once, and the chance of at least one false flag rises to about \(1 - (1 - \alpha)^k\), for example 34% for k = 8 at alpha = 0.05, even when every uncorrected p-value is calibrated. The corrected p-value controls this. correction = "fwer" bounds the probability of any false flag (strict, less power), and "fdr_bh" and "fdr_by" bound the expected share of false flags among those raised. Use the uncorrected p-value for a single comparison chosen in advance, and a corrected one when screening the whole table, which is the usual case.

Flags depend on the other items

Item infit and item-restscore both judge each item against expectations from a Rasch model fitted to all items, so misfitting items change what is expected of the others. A flag in one direction can therefore produce flags in the other. Overfitting items can push fitting items into the underfit range, and underfitting items, for example from a second dimension, can make fitting items look overfit. How large the effect is depends on how strong the misfit is and how many items share it. In simulation with seven polytomous items, two overfitting items led to about 6% of the fitting items being flagged as underfit, and one or two mildly multidimensional items to 1% to 2% being flagged as overfit. When items are flagged in both directions, consider removing the clearest misfit and testing again before interpreting the rest.

References

Ferreira, J. A. (2024). Methods of testing a 'small' or 'moderate' number of hypotheses simultaneously. Journal of Statistical Theory and Practice, 19(1), 6. doi:10.1007/s42519-024-00412-4

Kreiner, S. (2011). A Note on Item–Restscore Association in Rasch Models. Applied Psychological Measurement, 35(7), 557–561. doi:10.1177/0146621611410227

See also

RMitemRestscoreCutoff() for the simulations, RMitemRestscorePlot() to plot them, RMitemRestscoreBoot() for large samples, and RMitemInfit() for a second item fit test.

Examples

# \donttest{
if (requireNamespace("iarm", quietly = TRUE)) {
  # Simulate binary item response data (8 items, 200 persons)
  set.seed(42)
  sim_data <- as.data.frame(
    matrix(sample(0:1, 200 * 8, replace = TRUE), nrow = 200, ncol = 8)
  )
  colnames(sim_data) <- paste0("Item", 1:8)

  # Default kable output
  RMitemRestscore(sim_data)

  # Sorted by absolute difference
  RMitemRestscore(sim_data, sort = "diff")

  # Return as data.frame for further processing
  df <- RMitemRestscore(sim_data, output = "dataframe")

  # Bootstrap null distribution, flagging on Westfall-Young corrected
  # p-values (use 1000 or more iterations in a final analysis)
  if (requireNamespace("ggdist", quietly = TRUE)) {
    cutoff_res <- RMitemRestscoreCutoff(sim_data, iterations = 100,
                                        parallel = FALSE, seed = 42)
    RMitemRestscore(sim_data, cutoff = cutoff_res)
  }
}
